q: A stakeholder asks for a 'smarter bot' without naming intents, fields, or success criteria. Correct next step before architecture?
options: Translate the request into concrete functional requirements: which intents, which fields, and what counts as a correct outcome
Start coding against the largest model so capability covers whatever 'smarter' turns out to mean
Write the system prompt first and reverse-engineer requirements from its behaviour
Skip requirements and jump to MCP server selection
why: Vague business language must become checkable functional requirements before design. Oversizing the model or prompting first skips the step that makes the system testable.

q: Which activity belongs to operate-and-maintain, not design or build?
options: Monitoring production quality and cost, and triaging regressions as usage or models shift
Writing the initial functional requirements
Selecting the prototype model tier
Designing the first-release eval suite
why: Operate-and-maintain is post-launch monitoring and response to drift. Requirements, tier choice, and initial eval design happen earlier.

q: Which TWO statements about the Messages API are accurate? (Pick 2)
options: It is the primary conversational request surface for system, user, assistant, and tool turns
Client SDKs wrap the same REST Messages API rather than replacing it with a proprietary protocol
Streaming responses cannot include tool calls
max_tokens caps input history size, not output
why: Messages API is the main chat/tool surface; SDKs wrap the same REST API. Tool calls do stream, and max_tokens caps output not history.

q: Under burst load you see both 429 and 529 responses. Which TWO client behaviours are appropriate? (Pick 2)
options: Backoff and retry with jitter on both, treating them as transient capacity signals
Treat 429 as 'never retry' and 529 as a permanent model failure
Cap concurrent in-flight requests and respect Retry-After when present
Disable authentication so rate limits no longer apply
why: 429 and 529 are capacity/overload signals: retry with backoff/jitter, limit concurrency, and honour Retry-After. They are not permanent failures, and removing auth does not fix rate limits.

q: You need live moderation under 1s SLA and a monthly archive re-score with no user waiting. How should API modes split?
options: Synchronous Messages calls for live moderation; Message Batches for the monthly archive job
Batches for both to keep one code path
Synchronous for both to avoid maintaining two paths
Streaming for the monthly job because streaming is always cheapest
why: Match SLA: realtime needs sync; latency-tolerant bulk belongs on Batches. Forcing one path sacrifices latency or cost.

q: Which TWO describe Message Batches results correctly? (Pick 2)
options: You poll for completion then retrieve results within the processing window
Individual items can succeed or fail independently
Results stream live over a held-open connection as each item finishes
One failed item rolls back and refunds the entire batch
why: Batches are async poll-then-fetch; per-item success/failure. There is no live held-open result stream, and one failure does not roll back the batch.

q: A large stable system prompt is followed by a daily-changing user profile then the question. How maximise cache hits without caching stale profile data forever as one blob?
options: Place cache breakpoints so the stable system prompt is cached separately from the profile segment
Cache the entire assembled prompt as one block and accept full misses whenever the profile changes
Disable caching because any dynamic field invalidates the mechanism entirely
Move the profile after the question so order no longer matters for caching
why: Multiple breakpoints let stable prefixes stay cached while dynamic segments invalidate independently. One mega-block or disabling caching wastes the stable win.

q: When should a streamed assistant turn be committed to conversation history?
options: Only after message_stop confirms completion; discard partial turns on interruption
As soon as the first content_block_start arrives
When the HTTP socket closes for any reason
After the first text delta token
why: Socket close or early events are not completion. Commit only after message_stop so history never stores half-built turns.

q: An inspector app sends four photos and asks Claude to compare them. Correct request structure?
options: All four as image blocks in one message with the text instruction so the model sees them together
Four separate conversations then a fifth merge call, because a message may hold only one image
Paste image URLs as plain text only
Convert all four to a single PDF first; raw multi-image is unsupported
why: A single message can carry multiple image blocks plus text for direct comparison. Splitting or URL-as-text loses the multimodal comparison.

q: A one-off product photo is analysed once; a brand watermark is reused on thousands of requests. How should each be supplied?
options: Inline the one-off as base64; serve the reused watermark via the Files API so it is not re-uploaded every call
Inline both as base64 every time because the repeated bytes are negligible at scale
Describe both in text to avoid image tokens always
Force both through Batches regardless of latency
why: Files API fits reused assets; inline base64 fits one-offs. Re-inlining a watermark wastes tokens every call.

q: A support tool reuses one long-running Claude conversation for all customers 'to preserve context.' What is wrong?
options: Cross-customer leakage: each user or case needs its own conversation with only its own context
Nothing, if the context window is large enough
Only latency suffers; privacy is unaffected
It only breaks prompt caching
why: Shared conversations bleed one customer's data into another's answers. Window size does not fix session hygiene.

q: The same feature must work in claude.ai, via the API, and in Claude Code. A teammate assumes one prompt behaves identically everywhere. Flaw?
options: Each surface wraps prompts with different default context and instruction handling, so identical wording can still diverge
There is no flaw; behaviour is guaranteed identical across interfaces
Only the API supports system prompts
Claude Code ignores system prompts entirely
why: Surfaces layer different defaults around the same words. System prompts exist across surfaces; identical behaviour is not guaranteed.

q: Plugin A requires plugin B at 2.x but the project pins B at 1.x. What kind of problem is this?
options: A plugin dependency conflict that must be resolved by aligning versions or isolating plugins before production trust
Harmless duplication because plugin versions are cosmetic
A pure load-time performance issue
Something the model silently arbitrates at runtime
why: Conflicting version requirements are dependency conflicts needing explicit resolution, like any software graph.

q: You invoke Claude through a cloud vendor's hosted endpoint rather than first-party Anthropic. What stays true?
options: Messages API shape is generally consistent, but auth, headers, and some access patterns can differ by vendor
Vendors run an unrelated model that only shares the marketing name
Streaming is first-party only
Tool use is unavailable on vendor endpoints
why: Vendor hosting usually preserves Messages API shape while differing in platform auth/details. Streaming and tools are not first-party exclusives.

q: A 2,000-line prompt-handling function is unreadable and every change risks regressions. Appropriate response?
options: Refactor incrementally into smaller tested functions with clear responsibilities rather than a blank-file rewrite
Leave it; prompt code cannot be structured
Rewrite from scratch in one sitting with no tests
Add a long comment and keep extending the monolith
why: Incremental, tested refactoring is the standard fix for SRP violations. Untested rewrites and comments do not restore structure.

q: Two engineers merge Claude-calling features into the same file in one sprint with no review. Missing SDLC practice?
options: Code review in the merge process to catch conflicting assumptions before production
A larger context window so each engineer sees the other's edits automatically
A bigger model to resolve merge conflicts
Prompt caching to prevent git conflicts
why: Code review is the human gate that catches colliding assumptions. Model size and caching do not replace review.

q: Production pins a dated model ID. A new dated release documents a breaking change for your prompts. Which TWO actions fit a controlled upgrade? (Pick 2)
options: Run evals and canaries on the new ID before switching the pin
Update the pinned ID only after comparing outputs and costs against the reliability floor
Switch the floating alias in production first so customers get the new model immediately
Delete all regression tests because model upgrades never change behaviour
why: Pinned IDs enable deliberate upgrades: validate with evals/canaries and check quality/cost before changing the pin. Jumping floating aliases in prod and dropping tests defeat control.

q: A teammate says using the Anthropic SDK means you are no longer calling the REST API. Accurate statement?
options: The SDK wraps the same REST API with typing, retries, and auth helpers; wire calls remain HTTP
The SDK uses a proprietary binary protocol that bypasses HTTP
The SDK runs the model locally
Raw REST is unsupported once an SDK exists
why: SDKs are ergonomic clients over the same REST surface. Raw HTTP remains valid.

q: A workload mixes trivial FAQ calls with occasional hard multi-constraint planning. One config should spend reasoning only where warranted. Best fit?
options: Adaptive thinking so effort scales with the task
Maximum extended thinking on every call
Fast mode on every call
Human routing between two deployments for each request
why: Adaptive thinking scales effort per task. Always-max overpays; always-fast underserves hard cases.

q: A latency-sensitive FAQ endpoint does not need step-by-step reasoning. Correct thinking posture?
options: Leave extended/adaptive deep reasoning off unless a reasoning pass would change the answer
Pin maximum effort on every call for safety
Always route to the largest model tier
Enable thinking but delete thinking blocks before the next turn
why: Spend reasoning only where it changes outcomes. Max effort or largest tier on trivial traffic wastes cost and latency.

q: Across multi-turn extended thinking, what must happen to thinking blocks?
options: Return them unchanged on subsequent turns or the exchange breaks
Summarise them to save context while keeping the gist
Delete them before the next call
Move them into the system prompt
why: Thinking blocks must be echoed unchanged. Summarising, deleting, or relocating them breaks multi-turn thinking.

q: Production behaviour changed overnight with no deploy. Config uses a floating model alias. Likely cause and fix?
options: The alias moved to a newer release; pin a dated version and promote upgrades after evals
The API silently retrained on your traffic; opt out in the console
Temperature drifted upward automatically
Prompt cache served another customer's completions
why: Floating aliases follow new releases. Pin dated versions for deliberate upgrades.

q: Finance needs per-feature Claude spend and you have no numbers yet. First practical step?
options: Log the usage fields (input/output tokens) from each API response per feature
Estimate from character counts alone
Split the monthly invoice evenly across features
Enable extended thinking to get richer billing detail
why: Responses report token usage; per-feature logging yields real numbers. Even splits and char guesses hide drivers.

q: Prompt caching hit rate is near zero. Prompt order is [today's date] + [profile] + [20k policy manual] + [question]. Why?
options: Dynamic date and profile precede the stable manual, so the prefix never matches; put stable content first
Caching requires Batches and cannot work synchronously
20k tokens exceeds any cacheable size
Caching only applies to output tokens
why: Cache keys on identical prefixes. Leading dynamic content breaks hits; stable-first ordering fixes it.

q: Legal nuance summarisation vs fast internal wiki lookup. How should model tiers differ?
options: Higher-capability tier for nuanced legal work; faster cheaper tier for simple retrieval
Same highest tier for both for consistency
Cheapest tier for both to control cost uniformly
Tier choice does not matter if prompts are identical
why: Match tier to difficulty: nuance justifies capability; simple retrieval does not need it.

q: What is the 'reliability floor' in a cost-and-latency design section?
options: The minimum reliability you refuse to trade away for cost or speed
The lowest cost if you accept arbitrary dropped requests
The cheapest model SKU
The p99 latency target alone
why: Reliability floor is the non-negotiable reliability bound, not a cost or latency number.

q: When should hard cost and latency budgets be set?
options: Before architecture is locked so designs can be checked against them
Only after production profiling under real traffic
Only after the first cost overrun
At the first incident review
why: Budgets must shape architecture before build. Waiting until after means they never constrained design.

q: A nightly ETL always runs the same five steps in fixed order. Right architecture and why?
options: A workflow: the path is known, so coding it avoids agent cost and nondeterminism
An agent for future-proofing even though the path never branches
One mega-prompt listing all steps unordered
Five independent unordered calls
why: Known fixed sequences are workflows. Agents add nondeterminism you do not need.

q: A hard-coded invoice workflow breaks on unpredictable new supplier formats. Architectural signal?
options: The variable portion now warrants a bounded agentic decision; pure branching races new formats forever
Add a new hard-coded branch for every new supplier forever
The model tier is simply too small
Replace everything with one large prompt
why: When inputs leave the codeable path, agent territory appears for the variable part—not endless branches.

q: In a manager/supervisor hierarchy, what is the manager's job?
options: Decompose the goal, delegate to specialised subagents, and integrate results
Execute every subtask while subagents only observe
Enforce API rate limits only
Cache subagent prompts only
why: Managers decompose, delegate, and integrate. They are not the sole executors nor mere infra helpers.

q: An agent can permanently delete customer records. Correct design-time control?
options: A human approval gate before the delete executes
Logging and alerts after deletes so on-call can recover
Lower temperature only
A system-prompt reminder to be careful
why: Irreversible actions need a pre-execution human gate. Logs after the fact are too late.

q: A research agent must synthesise 40 documents but one shared context degrades quality. Best approach?
options: Subagents extract per document in isolation, then synthesise from compact extracts
Load all 40 and raise max_tokens as high as possible
Drop documents that do not fit
Lower temperature only
why: Isolated subagent contexts keep extracts clean. Cramming all documents is the bloat that hurt quality.

q: You are choosing self-hosted agent infrastructure versus an Anthropic-hosted managed agent. Core tradeoff?
options: Self-hosting maximises infra/data-flow control at operating cost; managed reduces ops burden with less infra control
There is no meaningful difference
Self-hosting is always cheaper regardless of team capacity
Managed hosting is only for non-agentic chat
why: The tradeoff is control and operational burden versus convenience—not identical options.

q: Which TWO are established agent patterns for multi-step work? (Pick 2)
options: A tool-use loop that calls tools and folds results until done
Delegating a bounded subtask to a subagent that returns a compact result
Hard-coding every possible input branch so no runtime decision exists
Disabling all tools to force pure parametric knowledge
why: Tool-use loops and subagent delegation are core patterns. Exhaustive hard branches and disabling tools are not.

q: Hand-rolling state, retries, and branching across eight agent steps has become spaghetti. What are LangGraph/Strands/PydanticAI for?
options: Orchestration: graph or typed control flow, explicit state, and retries so you stop hand-rolling plumbing
Fine-tuning the model to internalise the eight steps with no code
Replacing the need for tool schemas
Acting as vector databases
why: These frameworks structure multi-step control flow and recovery. They do not fine-tune models or replace tool schemas.

q: Over a long chat the JSON format specified early starts being ignored. Which technique addresses this failure type?
options: State and tighten the format rule durably in the system prompt
Attach reasoning few-shots to every user turn
Raise temperature
Swap models mid-conversation only
why: Cross-turn drift points to underspecified system instructions. Fix durability there, not with per-turn few-shot spam.

q: User text is concatenated into a prompt template and sometimes overrides instructions. Which TWO help at the prompt layer? (Pick 2)
options: Delimit and label user text clearly as data
Keep trusted instructions in the system prompt, separate from user content
Ask users politely not to include instructions
Truncate all user input to 20 characters
why: Delimiting untrusted text and separating trusted system instructions blunt injection. Politeness and blunt truncation are weak or harmful.

q: Free-text user input flows into a prompt that also holds instructions. Beyond default model refusals, which TWO defences belong in the application layer? (Pick 2)
options: Separate untrusted user content structurally (e.g. tagged blocks / role boundaries) from system instructions
Validate and constrain model output before privileged side effects run
Concatenate user text into the system prompt so the model 'owns' both equally
Disable all logging so injection attempts cannot be investigated
why: Treat user text as untrusted and keep it separated from instructions; gate tools/actions on validated outputs. Merging into the system prompt and disabling logs worsen exposure.

q: RAG embeds entire 30-page docs as single chunks; answers are vague and context fills instantly. Fix?
options: Chunk into smaller semantically coherent passages so retrieval returns focused pieces
Keep whole-doc chunks but retrieve more of them
Only switch to a larger embedding model
Ask the model to ignore irrelevant parts while still paying for them
why: Whole-document chunks blunt precision and blow the budget. Smaller coherent passages fix granularity.

q: Parser breaks on valid JSON that includes a prose preamble. Most robust production handling?
options: Constrain to JSON-only with schema validation, and repair or reject before downstream use
Set temperature to 0 and trust formatting forever
Parse raw output without validation
Increase max_tokens so preambles have room
why: API/schema constraints plus defensive validation beat prompt-only hope. Temperature 0 does not enforce structure.

q: A critical instruction is buried mid six paragraphs of background and keeps being missed. Most direct fix?
options: Move the critical instruction to the start or end and trim unnecessary background
Duplicate the six background paragraphs
Lower temperature so the model 'reads more carefully'
Add another mid-document copy of the same buried line
why: Models attend more reliably at edges of long prompts; bury-less and trim noise.

q: Two tools both 'retrieve information' and Claude often picks the wrong one. Best single fix?
options: Add clear when-NOT-to-use guidance in each description
Rely on more distinctive parameter names alone while descriptions stay overlapping
Delete one tool immediately
Increase model tier only
why: Tool choice follows descriptions; exclusion conditions resolve overlap better than schema cosmetics.

q: A tool named handle_request does lookup, validation, and notification in one call; the agent is confused about results. Fix?
options: Split into focused single-responsibility tools with matching descriptions
Rename it to a more exciting name
Add a fourth responsibility
Only add a longer system-prompt example
why: Overloaded tools create ambiguity; split by responsibility.

q: An MCP server should expose a named parameterised 'weekly-report' template users invoke on demand. Which MCP primitive?
options: A prompt
A tool, because anything named is always a tool
A resource
A transport
why: Named user-invoked templates are MCP prompts. Tools are model-invoked actions; resources are readable data.

q: You connect three MCP servers. What must you manage?
options: Each server's tool definitions load into context whether used or not, adding cost
Connected servers forbid any custom tools in the same app
All three must use stdio
The context window permanently expands with no cost impact
why: Connected servers inject definitions into context regardless of use—connect deliberately.

q: A capability must call authenticated internal REST APIs and be reused across five apps, maintained by a platform team. Best approach?
options: An MCP server maintained centrally and connected by each app
A Skill duplicated into each repo
Five hand-synced custom tools
A pasted system-prompt block that cannot call APIs
why: Centralised live authenticated capability reuse is the MCP server case; Skills are instructional, not live API gateways.

q: A fetched page hides text telling the agent to email a file externally. Most effective mitigation?
options: Least privilege so the summariser has no email capability, plus isolating untrusted content from instructions
Only a system-prompt line to ignore embedded instructions
Keyword-scan for 'ignore'
Switch to a larger more compliant model
why: Durable defense is capability removal and isolation. Prompt-only and keyword scans are bypassable.

q: A triage assistant receives full customer records but only needs message text and product name. Which TWO practices apply? (Pick 2)
options: Send only needed fields, stripping the rest before the API call
Redact or tokenise identifiers that must pass through
Send the full record but tell the model not to read sensitive fields
Encrypt the API key more strongly instead of minimising prompt data
why: Data minimisation and redaction keep unneeded PII out. Instructing the model to ignore fields still transmits them.

q: User jailbreak attempt vs malicious instructions hidden in a fetched page. How do they differ?
options: Jailbreak is direct user policy bypass; injection arrives via untrusted third-party content—mitigations differ
They are identical attacks with one identical fix
Authenticated users make jailbreaks harmless
HTTPS makes page-borne injection impossible
why: Direct jailbreaks vs content injection need different layers (policy/refusal vs isolation/least privilege).

q: Content policy lives only as one system-prompt line. Secure-by-design improvement?
options: Layer independent controls: prompt guidance plus output filtering plus scoped tool permissions
Make the prompt line longer and stop there
Remove the prompt line as useless
Rely on users to self-police
why: Layered guardrails avoid a single probabilistic point of failure.

q: First pass on an untrusted third-party repo. Correct permission posture?
options: Read-only plan mode to explore and propose before edits
bypassPermissions for uninterrupted speed
Manual approval of every file read
Disable all tools
why: Match authority to risk: plan mode explores without writing. bypassPermissions grants too much too early.

q: A PreToolUse hook must block a disallowed read. Which TWO are true? (Pick 2)
options: PreToolUse fires before the tool executes, so it can block
Exit code 2 with a reason on stderr signals the block
PostToolUse can also prevent the read by undoing it
Exit 0 with a reason on stdout blocks the call
why: Only PreToolUse can block; exit 2 + stderr is the block signal. PostToolUse is too late; exit 0 allows.

q: An agent quotes the wrong price. The trace shows the pricing tool returned the correct number. Where is the failure?
options: In how the model used the correct tool data, not in the tool itself
Always in the integration layer whenever a final answer is wrong
In the network
In API key configuration
why: Correct tool data plus wrong final answer isolates model reasoning/use of the data.

q: A client-side tool reads the user's current form field; a server-side tool queries a production database. A refactor swaps their execution locations. What breaks first?
options: The client-state tool can no longer see browser state once forced server-side
Nothing; tools are interchangeable regardless of execution location
Only latency changes; both still function identically
The database tool becomes faster and more secure on the client
why: Execution follows where data lives: live browser state is invisible to the server. Swapping locations breaks access, not merely latency.

q: Which TWO success criteria are specific enough to build an eval against? (Pick 2)
options: Return valid JSON with sentiment in {positive, negative, neutral} and confidence in [0,1]
Classify the ticket into exactly one of five named categories
Produce a genuinely useful triage
Handle the ticket well
why: Constrained JSON and a closed category set are checkable. 'Useful' and 'handle well' are too vague to grade.
